Banded bead anemone

Anthopleura

1-2cm. One row of tapered tentacles with a banded pattern. Large oral relative to tentacles. Usually brownish. On rocky shores, in sand or in cracks in large boulders and sea walls. Commonly seen on our shores.

Spotted mangrove anemone

Less than 0.5cm, at low tide, a tiny blob with 'eye spots': black centre with white and orange edges. Among barnacles, wood on the high shore among mangroves.

Striped bead anemone

Paracondylactis singaporensis

2-3cm. Abut 40 tentacles with dark stripes and white bars. On hard surfaces and rocky shores. Common on our Northern shores.

Swimming anemone

Boloceroides memurrichi

Branched-tentacle mangrove anemone

Pelocoetes exul

2-3cm. Few transparent tentacles, that branch at least once ending in tapering tips, with narrow white rings at the branching point. Oral disk tiny. Body column pale. Sometimes seen on mudflats near mangroves and freshwater flows on our Nothern shores.

Pink-spotted bead anemone

Anthopleura buddemeieri

1-2cm. Pale column with pink spots in rows. One row of tapered tentacles pale, greyish with pinkish cast. Near high water mark on bouldery rocky shore under rich coastal forest. Seen on our Southern shores.

Lined bead anemone

Diadumene lineata

Less than 0.5cm, at low tide, a tiny blob with fine stripes in white, orange, yellow or red. Among barnacles, on jetty legs and other hard surfaces. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Big hermit-hitching anemone

Calliactis

2-3cm. Many short tapering tentacles. Oral disk with fine white stripes. Body column thick, long with broad dark bars. On shells occupied by hermit crabs. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Small hermit-hitching anemone

identification*

1-2cm. Many short tapering tentacles. Oral disk white or with white radiating stripes. Body column short, smooth and not covered in sediments, pale some with faint stripes. On shells occupied by hermit crabs. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Seagrass anemone

Less than 1cm. Many translucent tentacles with tiny spots, body column short with tiny bumps. Sometimes seen stuck on seagrasses on some of our shores.

Snail-hitching anemone

Paraiptasia radiata

1cm. On living snails. Many long thin tentacles. Body brown with pale stripes. On shells of living snails. Sometimes seen on some of our shores.

Brain anchor coral

Euphyllia ancora*

Colonies 10-20cm. Corallites forming meandering valleys with separate walls. Tentacles with a U-shaped tip. Colours blue and brown with bluish tips. Seen on our Southern shores.

Torch anchor coral

Euphyllia glabrescens

Colonies 10-20cm. Corallites trumpet-shaped. Tentacles with rounded tips. Colours beige, brown and blue. Sometimes seen on our Southern shores.

Branching anchor corals

Euphyllia paraancora*

Colonies 10-20cm. Corallites trumpet-shaped. Tentacles with U-shaped tips. Colours green, brown and purple with white or bluish tips. Seen on our Southern shores.

Frog spawn coral

Euphyllia paradivisa*

Colony 10-20cm. Corallites trumpet-shaped. Tentacles are branched at the tips into masses of rounded and U-shaped tips. Colours green and brown with white or bluish tips. Rarely seen, on our Southern shores

Pearl bubble coral

Physogyra lichtensteini*

Colony 10-20cm. Corallites brain-like meandering made up of large coin-like disks. In daylight covered in bubbles. Colours beige. Rarely seen, on our Southern shores

Ball-tip corallimorphs

Corynactis

This small animal with little balls at the tips of its transparent tentacles is seen growing on hard surfaces. Rocks and coral rubble in clusters of a few individuals. Sometimes seen on some of our shores.

Beaded corallimorph

Discosoma nummiforme

This little disk-like animal with round bead-like bumps is sometimes seen in small groups on coral rubble on many of our Southern shores.

Carpet corallimorph

Rhodactis indosinensis

This shaggy disk-shaped animal is commonly encountered on many of our Southern shores, on coral rubble.

Corallimorphs

Frilled corallimorph

Rhodactis inchoata

This little animal with a delicate fringe around the edge of its disk-shaped body is sometimes encountered on our Southern shores, in coral rubble areas.

Ridged corallimorph

Platyzoanthus mussoides

These little ridged disk-like animal is sometimes seen on our Southern shores, growing on coral rubble.

Striped corallimorph

Discosoma

These little brown disk-shaped animal with stripes is sometimes encountered on our Southern shores, in coral rubble areas.

Stubby corallimorph

Ricordea yuma

These little disk-shaped animal with stubby tentacles is sometimes encountered on our Southern shores, among coral rubble.

White-tip corallimorphs

Rhodactis indosinensis

This small animal with white bulbous tips on its tentacles is often seen in clusters of several tucked among dead and living corals. Sometimes seen on some of our Southern shores.

Leathery soft corals

Soft corals

Broad feathery soft coral

Sansibia flava*

Colony 5-10cm,. Polyps 1cm in diameter on stalks 0.5-2cm long. Eight broad tentacles with thick side branches. Beige, pink, pale powder blue to bright blue, entire animal the same colour. The polyps don't pulsate. On stones in coral rubble. Commonly seen on our Southern shores.

Brown feathery soft coral

Colony 10-15cm. Polyps 1-1.5cm in diameter, on stalks 1-2cm long. Eight skinny tentacles with long thin side branches. Side branches pale brown, oral disk and main tentacles paler. The polyps don't pulsate. On coral rubble. Seen on our Southern shores.

Fine feathery soft coral

Briareum excavatum

Colony 10-15cm. Polyps about 1cm in diameter, on stalks about 1cm long. Eight skinny tentacles with short thin side branches. Side branches brownish, oral disk and tentacles white, greenish or bluish. The polyps emerge from an encrusting purple common membrane. The polyps don't pulsate. On coral rubble. Seen on our Southern shores.

Knobbly soft coral

Carijoa

Black-and-white leathery soft coral

Cladiella

Omelette leathery soft coral

Sarcophyton

Pimply leathery soft coral

Lobophytum

Pinwheel leathery soft coral

Lobophytum

Smooth leathery soft coral

Sinularia

Starry leathery soft coral

Sinularia

Asparagus flowery soft coral

Nephthea

Colony bushy 15-20cm, branched with study 'stems' that re white, lilac or purple. Polyps tiny (about 0.5cm) with eight beige or brown branched tentacles, appear in clusters at the tips of the branches. Among living hard corals on the reef flat. Commonly seen on our Southern shores.

Ball flowery soft coral

Dendronephthya sp.*

Colony spherical 6-10cm with a fat central 'trunk' that branches densely. The 'stem' white or transparent, pink or orange at near the polyp clusters. Polyps tiny (about 0.5cm) with eight white branched tentacles and tiny spikes nearby. On coral rubble. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Flowery soft corals

Pink flowery soft coral

Dendronephthya sp.*

Colony tree-like 10-15cm, branched with sturdy 'stems' that are white or transparent, embedded with red or pink spicules. Polyps tiny (about 0.5cm) with eight white branched tentacles. No spikes next to the polyps. On boulders, hard surfaces, coral rubble. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Smooth flowery soft coral

Litophyton

Colony bushy 6-12cm, branched with 'stems' that are white or transparent, embedded with spicules. Polyps tiny (about 0.5cm) with eight branched tentacles, may be beige, white or purple. No spikes next to the polyps. On coral rubble. Uncommon.

Spiky flowery soft coral

Stereonephthya

Colony bushy 6-12cm, branched with 'stems' that are white or transparent, embedded with spicules. Polyps tiny (about 0.5cm) with eight branched tentacles, may be beige, white or purple. Large spikes next to the polyps. On coral rubble. Seen on our Northern shores.

Xenia soft coral

Heteroxenia

Colony 5-10cm. Polyps about 2cm in diameter, on stalks about 3-5cm long. Eight skinny tentacles with short thin side branches. Side branches brownish, oral disk and tentacles pinkish. The polyps emerge from a common membrane. The polyps may pulsate. On coral rubble. Seen on our Southern shores.

Asparagus sea fan

Dichotella cf.

15-20cm. Colony is a cluster of strems. Stems cylindrical, unbranched except near the base, covered with bumps, large white polyps emerge from tips of bumps. Red, white, yellow or orange. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Blue sea fan

15-20cm. Colony with long branches. Cylindrical stems white or pink with large blue polyps all around. On coral rubble, rocks. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Candelabra sea fan

Euplexaura

10-15cm. Colony with sparse branches, that emerge in a U-shape. Cylindrical stems with large white polyps all around. Orange. On coral rubble, rocks. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Flat branch sea fan

Subergorgia

10-20cm. Colony randomly branched, on one plane. Stems flattened with groove along the centre, large white polyps at sides of stem, not in groove. Brown, orange, red. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Gnarled sea fan

Echinomuricea pulchra*

10-15cm. Colony few branching stems on one plane, cylindrical stems with large pink polyps. On coral rubble. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Sea fans or Gorgonians

Leathery sea fan

identification*

20-30cm. Colony bushy, long stems not frequently branched. Cylindrical, thick (1cm) fleshy and leathery, with a wire-like central support sometimes exposed at the tips. Dusky pinkish beige. On coral reefs. Seen on our Southern shores.

Lemon sea fan

15-20cm. Colony with long branches, tangled in large colonies. Cylindrical stems white or pale with large yellow or pale orange polyps all around. On coral rubble, rocks. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Lyre sea fan

Ctenocella pectinata*

15-20cm. Colony with long unbranched thin cylindrical stems emerging vertically from a horizontal stem. Red or brown. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Maze sea fan

Echinogorgia

10-15cm. Colony with regular branches that form a maze-like pattern. Fat cylindrical stems. Orange, pink, yellow or white. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on our Nothern shores.

Skinny sea fans

Astrogorgia

10-20cm. Colony with branches on one plane that resemble veins of a leaf, or long tangled stems. Relatively large white polyps on opposite edges of the flattened, skinny stems. Red, maroon, orange, yellow. On coral rubble, rocks, in sand. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Tree sea fan

10-15cm. Colony with branches on one plane that resembles the silhouette of a large tree. With swollen nodes where stems branch. Polyps all around the stem. Red, pink or white. On coral rubble, rocks, in sand. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Sea whip

Junceella sp.*

20-30cm. Cylindrical stem unbranched, small white or transparent polyps. White or yellow. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Blue coral

Heliopora coerulea

Candy hydroid

awaiting identification

5-10cm long with small capsules along the side branches. Pink or orange. On boulders, jetties. Commonly seen on some of our Northern shores.

Delicate hydroid

awaiting identification*

Clusters of many tiny fans, that can cover an area of about 5-10cm. Each tiny fan about 0.5cm in diameter. Pale brown. Colonies of these tiny animals are often encountered on our Southern shores, but often overlooked. In coral rubble areas.

Fluffy hydroid

awaiting identification*

10-15cm long densely branching with fine 'stems'. Usually bright orange. On coral rubble. Sometimes seen on some of our Northern shores.

Giant hydroid

awaiting identification*

2m or longer. Unbranched feather. Usually in deeper water on our Southern shores. Sometimes fragments are washed ashore.

Hydroids

awaiting

Seagrass hydroid

awaiting identification*

0.5cm or shorter. Feathery, grows in rows on seagrass blades. Sometimes seen on some of our shores.

Fern hydroid

awaiting identification*

10-15cm long forming a fern-like shape. Usually bright orange. On boulders and coral rubble. Sometimes seen on some of our Northern shores.

Stinging hydroid

awaiting identification*

4-20cm long. Transparent or white fern-like 'leaves' on black branches. Stings powerfully. On coral rubble. Commonly seen on some of our shores.

Thread-tentacled jellyfish

Aequorea

Bell about 10cm across, thin thread-like tentacles about 25cm long. Sometimes seen on some of our shores.

Fat-armed jellyfish

Catostylus

Bell 6-10cm across, short thick fat tentacles. Sometimes seen on our Northern shores.

Huge jellyfish

Bell about 25-50cm across, short tentacles. Sometimes seen washed ashore or trapped in pools on our Northern shores.

Jellyfish

Mangrove jellyfish

Acromitus

Bell 6-8cm across, short thick fat tentacles with thin 'tails'. Sometimes seen in mangrove streams and lagoons in our Northern shores.

Ribbon jellyfish

Chrysaora

Bell 8-12cm across, ribbon-like tentacles 20-50cm long. Sometimes seen on our shores. Stings painfully.

Upsidedown jellyfish

Cassiopea

Bell about 4-12cm, tentacles length about half the bell diameter. Usually seen upside down. Can be seasonally common on Pulau Semakau and shores near the island.

Sea pencil

Lituaria

4-10cm long. Stiff white cylindrical central stalk bears transparent secondary polyps (less than 1cm) that have branched tentacles. When exposed at low tide, the secondary polyps are retracted and they look like fat pencils stuck in the sand. Sandy shores near seagrasses. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Sea pens

Spiky sea pen

Pteroeides sp.*

15-20cm long. Fat central stalk with short (2-3cm) leaf-like structures with tiny spikes on the edges. Secondary polyps tiny, on the edges of the leaf-like structure. White or beige. When exposed at low tide, the central stalk is often bent over into half. Sandy shores near seagrasses. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Flowery sea pen

15-20cm long. Sausage-like central stalk bears white flower-like secondary polyps (1-2cm) that have branched tentacles. Primary polyp thick and sausage-like. Maroon to orange, purple and white. When exposed at low tide, the secondary polyps are retracted and they look like limp sausages. Sandy shores near seagrasses. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Slender sea pen

Virgularia

15-20cm long. Stiff, narrow central stalk with short (1-2cm), leaf-like structures without spikes on the edges. Secondary polyps tiny, on the edges of the leaf-like structure. Maroon to orange, purple and white. When exposed at low tide, the stiff central primary polyp remains upright so they look like thin sticks stuck in the sand. Sandy shores near seagrasses. Commonly seen on our Northern shores.

Broad zoanthid

Palythoa mutuki

Colony 5-10cm, a cluster of a few individual polyps. Polyp 1-2cm with long body column, broad oral disk. On coral rubble. Commonly seen on our shores.

Pink button zoanthid

Zoanthus vietnamensis

Colony10-15cm, encrusting small stones and rubble. Polyps about 1cm with long body column tipped in bright pink. Sometimes seen on our shores.

Sea mat zoanthid

Palythoa tuberculosa*

Colony 20-40cm, encrusts rocks and rubble like a rubbery mat. Polyps 1-2cm in diameter embedded in this common tissue, short or no body column. Coral rubble, boulders. Commonly seen on our Southern shores.

Zoanthids

Button zoanthid

Zoanthus

Colony10-15cm, encrusting small stones and rubble sometimes forming dense carpet. Polyps about 1cm with long body column, oral disk appears to be split into two. Commonly seen on our shores.

Spoon shaped leaves, longer and the width, 0.5 wide, 1-2.5cm long, emerging in pairs. Minute serrations on edges and minute hairs on both sides of the leaves. Seen in deeper waters in our Southern islands.

Tape seagrass

Enhalus acoroides

Longest seagrass with ribbon-like leaves. 30cm-1.5m long, 1-2cm wide. Thick rhizomes. Flowering often observed. Large female flowers on coiled stalk. Tiny white male flowers produced from inflorescence at base of the plant. Often seen on most of our undisturbed shores. Largest meadow on Pulau Semakau.

Needle seagrass

Halodule

Thin ribbon-like leaves up to 15cm long and 3.5mm wide. Rhizomes thin. Sometimes seen on some our shores, especially on sand bars. Luxuriant growths seen on seaward sandbars on Chek Jawa.

Spoon seagrass

Halophila ovalis

Spoon shaped leaves, 0.5-1cm wide, 1-4cm long, emerging in pairs. Common on many of our shores.

Smooth ribbon seagrass

Cymodocea rotundata

Narrow and shorter ribbon-like leaves with rounded or squarish tips without serrations. Rhizomes thick and smooth. Seen on Chek Jawa, Tanah Merah and Cyrene Reef.

Seagrasses

Serrated ribbon seagrass

Cymodocea serrulata

Narrow and shorter ribbon-like leaves with rounded tips with fine serrations. Rhizomes thick and smooth. Seen on some of our Southern reefs and shores.

Fern seagrass

Halophila spinulosa

2cm wide, 4cm long. Only seagrass with opposite leaves on a stem that makes it appear fern-like. 10-20 opposite pairs of leaves on one stem, the stem about 4cm long. Rhizomes thin, sometimes woody. Common on Chek Jawa and Changi.

Noodle seagrass

Syringodium isoetifolium

Leaves cylindrical (like plastic tubing). Common on on Pulau Semakau.

Sickle seagrass

Thalassia hemprichii

Shorter and broader ribbon-like leaves that are curved into strap sickle shapes (4-11mm wide and 10-40cm long). Rhizomes thick. Small patch on Chek Jawa, larger meadows on Labrador, scattered clumps on some of our other Southern shores.
